rv.q: She makes the second act particularly thrilling, completing a character arc that is darkly funny and heartbreaking, holding the audience in the palm of her hand the entire time.
It all adds up to a show that’s more peculiar than provocative, as Owen’s reach exceeds his grasp.

Alas, anyone expecting even a fraction of the wit found in Edward Albee's similarly structured "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?" is bound to be sadly disappointed in Joshua Owen's "Human Things," now at the Theatre.
With sharp comedic turns, Human Things turns a remote island, an approaching storm, and two troubled marriages into an affecting night of theater.
The play is riveting- smart, imaginative and provocative.

cn.t: Joshua Owen's debut drama about two couples on a remote island before and after a catastrophic storm receives mixed reviews, with critics finding it overly ambitious in scope but falling short of the sharp wit it aspires to.
